A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GraLoRA, and their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison. The original method and experiments can be matched despite expanded evaluation and renumbering in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original code-generation and commonsense-reasoning experiments, alongside gradient, rank, memory, and training-time measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds mathematical reasoning, GLUE, image generation, and additional commonsense experiments. Some newly included baseline scores are explicitly attributed to prior work.

M1.justification: The blockwise GraLoRA construction, local adapter ranks, and Hybrid GraLoRA combination remain unchanged. Applying these methods to additional architectures does not establish a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: v2 adds MetaMathQA training with MATH evaluation, six GLUE tasks, and personalized image generation using Naruto-Blip-Captions. These substantially extend task and modality coverage beyond the retained code-generation and eight commonsense tasks. MNLI and QQP were not evaluated in v1, so their exclusion is not a removal.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds commonsense comparisons with Full-FT, LoRA-XS, LoRA-SB, MELoRA, rsLoRA, PiSSA, DoRA, BOFT, and LoRA-Pro; several scores are explicitly borrowed from Ponkshe et al. Table 7 additionally compares against VeRA and FourierFT on GLUE. The original LoRA, MoRA, and RaSA comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include rank-32 LLaMA3.2–3B commonsense evaluation, rank-8 RoBERTa GLUE experiments without MNLI-based transfer, and rank-128 SDXL training with a 90/10 split and CLIP/DINOv2 similarity metrics. Tables 9–10 specify additional training budgets and settings. Original benchmark settings are retained. Mathematical-model identity is inconsistent: Section 4.1 names LLaMA3.2–3B, while Tables 4 and 9 name Qwen2.5–1.5B.

E4.justification: The k sweep, hybrid-allocation sweep, gradient/outlier analyses, rank analysis, and resource comparisons are retained. Figure 8 corrects the presentation of the existing sweep rather than documenting a new analysis. The added appendix benchmark tables do not introduce a separate robustness or sensitivity study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new checklist explains that error bars were omitted because of computational expense, but does not change the statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: Original benchmark entries remain unchanged, while substantial new results appear. LLaMA3.2–3B commonsense averages are 84.6% for GraLoRA versus 81.3% for LoRA. Table 4 reports rank-128 MATH accuracy of 28.9% versus 24.7%. Tables 7–8 add GLUE and image-similarity results. The GLUE 86.0% 'Best GraLoRA' row combines taskwise maxima; individual GraLoRA and Hybrid averages are 85.8% and 85.6%.

T1.justification: v1 identifies both the true weight gradient and the reconstructed adapter update as dL/dR. Equations 2 and 4 in v2 distinguish these quantities, correcting their mathematical identification. The update algebra, rank argument, assumptions, and appendix FLOPs derivation remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains localized adaptation with greater effective rank and comparable computational cost. The abstract and conclusion extend the claimed empirical applicability from code generation and commonsense reasoning to mathematical reasoning, language understanding, and image generation.

C2.justification: New results sections interpret mathematical performance as evidence of usable higher-rank capacity and GLUE/SDXL performance as evidence of applicability beyond decoder language models. The original gradient-entanglement explanation and limitations concerning uniform partitioning and low-rank blocks remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix E substantially expands technical documentation through Tables 9–10, including optimizers, task-specific learning rates, classification-head learning rates, ranks, batches, and epochs; Section 4.1 adds hardware information. Conversely, v2 removes the explicit repository URL and original final-epoch checkpoint-selection statements. Its checklist asserts supplementary code availability without supplying a replacement repository address.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations supporting the new datasets and architectures, including MetaMath/MATH, GLUE/RoBERTa, and SDXL/Naruto, plus FourierFT and Ponkshe et al. The central positioning relative to LoRA and prior outlier research is largely unchanged; there is no substantial new related-work synthesis.

P1.justification: The experimental setup is reorganized, three results subsections and an additional-results appendix are inserted, and the former Appendix D becomes Appendix E. Acknowledgments and a conference checklist are added. Most existing introduction, method, analysis, and ablation prose remains substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands tabular presentation with mathematical, extended-baseline, GLUE, image-generation, and task-specific hyperparameter tables, while enlarging existing comparison tables. Figure 8 corrects the rank-group assignment and replaces three identical k=8 legend labels with k=2, 4, and 8. The other nine figures retain their content.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis for GraLoRA's generality: v1's evidence centered on two decoder-language-model domains, whereas v2 tests encoder and diffusion architectures and adds much broader PEFT and Full-FT comparisons. The gradient-definition and Figure 8 corrections also improve accuracy. These gains outweigh the new mathematical-model naming inconsistency and weaker code-access documentation, although the continued absence of uncertainty estimates limits confidence in small reported differences.
